newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's ACCC to have more power over telecoms.
newsitem.headline: Australia's ACCC to have more power over telecoms.

text.p: The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) will be given extra powers to ensure that groups adhere to the new laws in the soon-to-be deregulated telecommunications market, ACCC chairman Allan Fels said.

"The commission has been given a few extra big sticks to deal with potential problems particularly arising from Telstra," Fels said in a television interview on Nine Network's Sunday Business programme.
The government-owned telecommunications group Telstra holds a near monopoly of Australia's A$5 billion local call market, which will be open to full competition from July 1, 1997.

"We will have a competition notice power where we can issue a notice saying something is anti-competitive and if we aren't complied with there are fines of A$10 million, plus A$1 million a day for breaches if our views are upheld by the court," Fels said.
"So where we do act we have got a much bigger stick, but at the same time the approach is more practical and market- orientated," he said.
The anti-monopoly ACCC assumes the additional role as competition regulator of the telecommunications industry from July 1, 1997.

Telecommunications companies which plan to move into the Australian market post-July are likely to pay to connect to Telstra's national telephone network or to rival network owned by fellow telecom group Optus Communications Pty Ltd.
"There are quite substantial provisions in the act about access and interconnect and we are expecting to make some pretty significant decisions around July 1," Fels said.
